items.gist: The passage introduces the supreme word of Maheśa and distinguishes freedom within the light of Bhairava. The world is said to be nothing apart from that light.
A pure mirror reflects things without mixing, and purity is explained as non-difference from self-luminous consciousness. Touch is contrasted with sight to show that reflection is not mere contact.
Maya produces obstructive forms, while sadvidya is unobstructed. The Lord displays both kinds of manifestation as reflection and original.
The text rejects the claim that reflected light is merely external light bouncing back. It argues that reflection is an upaya and not a real separate entity in the mirror.
Mirror and reflected form are not ultimately distinct, and the mirror-instruction removes delusion. The passage denies fixed location, form, time, and other limiting properties.
Sound also has a reflection, called echo, and is heard by perceivers situated in the middle. Even without direct perception of the original, reflection can be grasped.
Echo depends on the mirror-like medium and is not heard from behind. Its manifestation and hearing occur in a coordinated, not merely delayed, manner.
The discussion extends reflection to touch, smell, taste, and other sense-objects. These are not perceived without the appropriate sense or medium.
Touch-reflection occurs through the internal instrument when external contact is impossible. The reflected touch produces a corresponding pleasant experience in the body.
The world is offered into consciousness as a reflection, taking on the Lord's pure universal form. Consciousness is the clearest medium, and reflection is established by reflection itself.
The text answers the objection that reflection requires an external original. It defines reflection as the appearance of another form without loss of one's own nature.
